forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Bolton to use £30m reserves over three years to bridge budget gap
news_drafts.lead: Bolton Council is planning to use £30m from its reserves over three years ending 2027 to bridge funding gaps, according to its medium-term financial strategy. The Audit Committee heard that external auditors have characterised the planned drawdown as "unsustainable reliance on reserves and a lack of action to address the underlying reasons for persistent overspending". Auditors identified that asset ceiling interest of £31.5m had not been included in the council's pension accounting, requiring a revised actuary report. They also raised control weaknesses across asset management and governance, including a failure to maintain the Corporate Risk Register during 2023–24. The council is receiving support from Manchester and Salford councils on internal audit delivery while developing a resource strategy to address staffing constraints.

news_drafts.headline: Bolton forecasts £10.5m overspend on schools grant for special needs in 2026-27, with a DfE plan pending
news_drafts.lead:
Bolton expects to spend £10.5m more than its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) in 2026-27, according to first-quarter monitoring papers for the council's Schools Forum. The whole of the overspend falls on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

The council forecasts high needs spending of £72.409m against a net budget of £61.869m. Schools' delegated budgets, the money passed directly to individual schools, are on plan. Adding this year's overspend to deficits carried forward, the central reserve for the grant (money set aside, here in deficit) is projected at negative £29.745m at 31 March 2027.

Bolton has submitted a plan to reform special educational needs provision to the Department for Education. The department's decision on it will determine whether Bolton receives a High Needs Sustainability Grant to address the deficit. The papers show a potential grant of £10.539m, matching the forecast overspend. Neither approval nor an award has yet been confirmed.

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: £135,325,000 of short-term investments are placed with other councils at interest rates of 4.25% to 4.80%.
findings.detail: Appendix 3 lists short-term deposits with other councils and one town council, with terms running to 2027. The listed rates range from 4.25% (Cornwall County Council) to 4.80% (Basildon District Council).
findings.matters: Councils lending to one another at these rates is a visible market signal to other finance officers and to lenders, showing where short-term cash is being placed.
findings.figures: £135,325,000 short-term investments; 4.25% to 4.80% interest rates; £10,000,000 per example deposit (Basildon District Council)

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: £118,000,000 (79.73%) of Bolton's borrowing falls due in the 30 to 35 year band, with no principal due in any band under 25 years.
findings.detail: The maturity profile shows £20,000,000 (13.51%) due in 25 to 30 years and £10,000,000 (6.76%) due in 45 to 50 years. Every band under 25 years shows zero, and the indicator is within the limits set in the Treasury Strategy.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk is spread across a small number of long-dated maturities, which a lender or another council's treasury team would want to see when assessing the borrower's exposure.

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: Bolton held £167,025,000 of investments at 30 September 2026 against £148.0m of external debt.
findings.detail: The paper states that investments represent the council's usable reserve balances and contingency funds, plus cash received in advance for later spending. Investments at 30 September 2026 total £167,025,000, of which £31,700,000 is in money market funds.
findings.matters: A reader can compare the cash held with the debt carried, which shows the council's liquidity position and how much of its reserves is held as cash.
findings.figures: £167,025,000 total investments; £148.0m external debt; £31,700,000 money market funds
findings.quote: The Council’s investments represent the Council’s usable reserve balances that are maintained to deliver services and provide contingency funds in the event of unforeseen circumstances.

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: The Bank of England base rate rose to 4% on 5 November 2026, ending six consecutive holds and the first rise in more than three years.
findings.detail: The paper says the base rate was 3.75% at 18 December 2025 and was increased to 4% on 5 November 2026. It sets this out as the context for the council's borrowing and investment position.
findings.matters: A finance director at Bolton or at another council would want to know that the rate on new borrowing and on cash deposits moved upward in this period.
findings.quote: On the 5 th November 2026 the base rate was increased to 4%, ending six consecutive holds and marking the first rise in more than three years.

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Deputy Leaders Portfolio
findings.headline: The paper gives the Bank of England base rate as 3.75% at 18 December 2025 and says financial markets are pricing a rise to around 4.0% by the end of 2026.
findings.detail: The paper reports that the base rate peaked at 5.25% in August 2023 and fell to 3.75% by 18 December 2025. It says current market expectations suggest a modest increase during 2026, to around 4.0% by year end.
findings.matters: Expected base rate movement bears directly on the cost of replacement borrowing and the return on short-term deposits, which a finance director or lender would model.
findings.figures: Base rate 5.25% peak in August 2023; 3.75% at 18 December 2025; market expectation around 4.0% by end of 2026.
findings.quote: financial markets pricing in a rise to around 4.0% by the end of the year
